metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against Tallying perfectly: on every single trial in the design, the two theories predict opposite choices. TTB relies solely on the first discriminating cue, while Tallying relies on the sheer number of winning cues. This metric simply computes the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction. Data generated by TTB will yield a value close to 1.0 (subject to noise), whereas data generated by Tallying will yield a value close to 0.0, making the two theories maximally discriminable.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the Tallying heuristic's prediction, restricted to trials where Tallying has a strict preference (i.e., one option has more feature wins than the other). By design, the experimental trials are structured such that whenever Tallying has a strict preference, Take The Best (TTB) makes the exact opposite prediction. Therefore, data generated by the Tallying model will yield values close to 1.0 (minus response noise), whereas data generated by the TTB model will yield values close to 0.0 (plus response noise). This extreme, diametric opposition guarantees a highly significant discrimination between the two theories.

The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Weighted Additive (WADD) model on critical trials where WADD and Tallying make strictly opposite predictions. Specifically, it isolates trials where one option possesses the two highest-validity features while the other possesses the three lowest-validity features. WADD's compensatory nature allows the two high-validity features to outweigh the three low-validity ones, predicting choice for the former. Tallying simply counts the winning features and predicts choice for the latter. The metric will be close to 1 for data generated by WADD and close to 0 for data generated by Tallying, providing maximal discrimination.

The metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing Option B between Trial 1 and Trial 6. In Trial 1, Option B is supported by 3 low-validity features while Option A is supported by 2 high-validity features. Tallying simply counts the features, favoring B (3 vs 2), whereas WADD integrates validities, strongly favoring A (0.95+0.9=1.85 vs 0.55+0.5+0.5=1.55). In Trial 6, the options are perfectly mirrored, so Tallying favors A and WADD favors B. Consequently, Tallying will yield a large positive difference (high P(B) on Trial 1, low P(B) on Trial 6), while WADD will yield a large negative difference. This creates a maximal contrast between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of times subjects choose the option that wins the most valid cue (feature 0) specifically on trials where the pure tally of feature wins is tied. Pure Tallying predicts a 50/50 guessing rate on these trials (metric ~ 0.5), while Hybrid Tallying predicts a systematic preference for the option winning the top cue (metric > 0.5). By isolating exactly the trials where the two theories diverge, we maximize the discriminative power of the metric.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the single most valid cue, strictly on trials where the overall tally is tied. Pure Tallying predicts a 50/50 guess on these trials since it ignores cue validities, resulting in an expected value of 0.5. Hybrid Tallying predicts a value significantly greater than 0.5 because it uses the top cue as a tie-breaker.
